A Levski Sofia supporter has been filmed appearing to perform a Nazi salute in the stands during Marseille’s Europa League tie against the Bulgarian side, in footage that has circulated widely online. The clip emerged amid chaotic scenes at the Stade Vélodrome , where flares and other projectiles were thrown and rival supporters clashed before and during Thursday’s match.
Around 500 Levski fans were housed in the away section. About ten minutes before kick-off , several Marseille supporters ran from a home stand and breached the away enclosure, apparently targeting the Bulgarian fans. Projectiles and flares were thrown between the two groups, and further disturbances broke out during the half-time break.
Five Levski Sofia supporters were taken to hospital with injuries including eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder, according to the Marseille police prefecture . Around a dozen Bulgarian fans were reportedly injured in total. Despite the disturbances, the match kicked off as scheduled, with Marseille securing a 1-0 victory over the Bulgarian side.
The violence drew condemnation from French President Emmanuel Macron and his Bulgarian counterpart, Iliana Iotova . Levski Sofia coach Julio Velázquez also condemned the incidents, describing the scenes as “unacceptable for football” . The disturbances overshadowed the European fixture and renewed concerns over spectator safety at international club matches.

This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk . Some carried broken lamps, glitching electronics, or cracked furniture. Others walked in with toolboxes, multimeters for testing electric currents, and cans of WD-40. Beneath extension cords dangling from the rafters, they sorted themselves into smaller groups: the volunteer electricians , tailors, luthiers, carpenters, and at least one cutler (knife sharpener), commandeering nearby worktables and passersby as needed.
That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.
“This is so interesting,” a giddy Pettus said, inspecting for the first time the joints, one of them broken, that held together the chair she’d owned for decades. “You never even know how furniture is put together.”
This is Decatur’s semi-regular repair café , one of a few hundred meetings like it across the United States. More Americans than ever are turning to these community gatherings to fix what they already own, resisting the influence of companies that sell everything from hiking boots to smartphones and hot water boilers and that push for replacement over repair. One consequence of this throwaway economy is an increase in greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing that threatens to intensify climate change.
Yet, organizers and volunteers consider repair cafés to be more than a relatively small climate solution. As inflation rises and wages stagnate, the meetups connect people to a movement with the ambitious goal of changing the fundamentals of America’s consumer economy .
At the Decatur repair café, volunteers, wearing green shirts with “I can probably fix that” printed on the back, offered their skills free of charge as patrons observed. A young father of a toddler and squirmy baby watched as a volunteer replaced a switch on a favorite mid-century modern lamp worn out by the older child’s repeated clicking. Murmurs of excitement rippled around the building as the acrid smell of a spot welding project wafted through.
Pettus’ broken chair held in its wood her family’s story. Soon after she and her husband were married in 1996, they began a search for a dining room set. Pettus wanted the chairs to be comfortable for her entire family, but one of her brothers is nearly 7 feet tall, and another just a few inches shorter. “We are not a tiny family,” Pettus said. “We are a big family.”
Pettus also thought of one of her children who’d interned at the Environmental Protection Agency and shared his concerns with Pettus about pollution and climate change. Then, after months of the broken chair cluttering the family’s house , Pettus was running Saturday morning errands when she passed the Decatur repair café. She drove the half-mile home to grab the chair and decided to give it a second chance.
“When a product breaks and you have to throw it away , it’s very lonely,” said Martine Postma, director of Repair Café International, a Netherlands-based network of 4,000 cafés. “ It’s easier to just go on the internet and order a new item which will come to your doorstep in 24 hours, but that’s also a very lonely, disconnected activity.”
Postma, a former journalist with the demeanor of an unflappable librarian, founded her organization in 2010 after the birth of her second child magnified her fears about the planet’s future . “Markets are flooded with trash—with cheap products that we don’t need and that do not work,” Postma said. “They break, and they contribute nothing to our well-being. They just contribute waste.”
Repair cafés appear to be inspiring people to use their stuff longer. In 2025, they prevented nearly 2 million pounds of waste—the equivalent of more than 100 fully loaded Boeing 747 aircraft —according to Repair Café International, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to the average consumption of about 1,000 Dutch families.
Postma, Pettus, and millions of others often smack into obstacles when they try to fix their own stuff. Broken products are increasingly difficult to repair, according to a report from the Federal Trade Commission titled “Nixing the Fix.” The report details how Americans are incentivized to “replace products before the end of their useful lives” by companies that decide to make repairs less safe, limit the availability of parts, lock software and firmware, or even “disparage” independent repair.
In 2023, California, Colorado, Minnesota, and New York passed “ right to repair ” legislation meant to encourage repair over replacement. A year later the European Union passed a similar directive. Postma and other organizers consider the cafés a natural place for activism to push for right-to-repair measures, although Postma hopes for more sweeping changes in Europe, like a tax on raw materials. She argued it would limit emissions and bolster repair shops, even if it increases the cost of products.
“ I feel for the objects around me. I feel sorry for them if they’re broken,” she said. “I want to make repairing a normal thing in everyday life once more.”
According to Postma, repairing goods is more common in relatively poor countries where replacing them can be especially difficult and expensive. It’s in wealthy countries that repair cafés are thriving, but they’re not at all uniform. Each reflects the surrounding area and its socioeconomics.
On a Sunday afternoon in the Collier Heights neighborhood of Atlanta, volunteers brought most of their own tools to the basement of a building owned by a Seventh-Day Adventist Church, setting them on white plastic folding tables atop a light pink carpet. The café looked much different from the one a 30-minute drive across the city in Decatur. The median annual household income in the mostly Black Collier Heights neighborhood is roughly $40,000 lower than in Decatur. Many people who brought items wanted them fixed less for sentimental reason, and more so they could keep using them.
Gale Pines walked in with a red air fryer that had stopped working after they used it to dehydrate ginger. When their oven ran, Pines said, it heated the entire kitchen. So, while in nursing school, they cooked many of their evening meals in the air fryer, most often chicken nuggets and fries.
Pines recently graduated but had trouble finding a job and couldn’t afford to buy a new $100 air fryer. “It’s just hard to exist,” Pines said. “I don’t really have a very big support network outside of my friends.”
One of Pines’ housemates told them about Collier Heights’ repair café. They keep a bag of broken electronics in the garage that they’d prefer not to send to a landfill. “Being in the height of climate collapse we can’t just keep buying new stuff all the time, both for the economy and for our material scarcity,” Pines said.
When a volunteer at the Collier Heights repair café opened up the air fryer, they quickly discovered the problem: a bad capacitor. Another volunteer had brought a replacement part, and the two of them made the fix as Pines watched, impressed, but unable to follow the relatively complex repair . Pines felt OK that they hadn’t learned how to fix the air fryer themself.
“ To just be around people that want to help other people with the skills that they have, that’s value that is really important to me and something that I try to do as well,” Pines said. “If somebody in my community has a question about their medication or something and can’t afford to go to the doctor, I’m happy to answer any questions that people have.”

We polled the Ars staff about their favorite pickups this year; here’s the list.
The holiday shopping season is upon us, and as is our custom, we’re here with a list of Ars staffers’ favorite recent purchases that could make good gifts. (Or maybe they might be a gift you get yourself!)
Rather than try to write a definitive “best gifts for your sister or brother” type of guide, we simply polled Ars staffers on stuff they’ve actually bought this year that they recommend. The thinking is that if we’re into it, hopefully some of you or your friends or family might be. As such, there’s no rhyme or reason to these selections, really; it’s just a list of stuff we bought that we’re happy about. It’s heavy on interesting books and cycling accessories, but there are some gadgets and the like in here, too.
For each gadget (or whatever else it might be), we have a brief description of how or why we’ve been using this particular thing and why we would recommend it. Our picks are ordered by price, from lowest to highest. Note, though, that the prices of these products are listed as they were when the list was written. Online retailers often adjust prices frequently, especially around Black Friday, so just a heads up: The price might be different by the time you read this.
Also, a callout to the Ars commentariat: If you have your own holiday buying recommendations, feel free to share them. We or some fellow readers might take your advice if you suggest something good! Happy holidays!
I understand the convenience and space-savings that e-readers bring. My 2011 Kindle Touch goes with me everywhere I carry my travel backpack, but I’m still a softy for physical books when I’m sitting at home on a lazy Sunday. What started as something of a fanfic send-up of LitRPGs has quickly blossomed into a massive sensation of a series filled with far more depth, heart, and character than the initial premise might indicate. Author Matt Dinniman has an accessible style that will grip any reader with a taste for whimsical adventure. Just be warned that if you leave the books under the tree, you might not see much of the recipient until New Year’s.
Undersea War: The Battle to Control the Cables and Pipelines That Connect Our World by Elisabeth Braw – $30
Lightning Beneath the Sea: The Race to Wire the World and the Dawn of the Information Age by James M. Tabor – $32
Two excellent books that help describe how the Internet’s undersea backbone became a globe-spanning reality were published in 2026. Together, they form a great gift pairing for anyone interested in how humanity first achieved near-instantaneous communication across the world’s oceans—and how the first trans-Atlantic telegraph cable paved the way for a global network of subsea data cables that now faces growing risks from geopolitical conflicts.
James Tabor’s Lightning Beneath the Sea dives into the astounding real-life story of how American entrepreneur Cyrus Field, lacking in expertise but driven by personal fervor, set out to achieve peace on Earth by laying a 2,000-mile telegraph cable made of copper across the Atlantic seafloor in 1866.
To pull off the feat, Field managed to convince some of the greatest innovators and scientific luminaries of his day, such as Samuel F.B. Morse, Lord Kelvin, and Michael Faraday, to join his venture. He also refitted the SS Great Eastern steamship, the largest passenger liner ship built to date, as a cable-laying vessel.
That first ocean-spanning telegraph cable gave rise to more such cables for transmitting messages around the world. Eventually copper gave way to a network of subsea fiber-optic cables that became the Internet’s undersea backbone, and the modern world also became interlinked with submarine power cables and underwater pipelines for carrying oil and gas.
But all that undersea infrastructure is now facing growing danger from the threat of deliberate sabotage, as described in Elisabeth Braw’s book Undersea War . Her book provides a sobering but enlightening look at why subsea cables and pipelines are becoming more tempting targets amid rising geopolitical tensions and conflicts—and how governments and companies are responding to recent cable-cutting incidents around the world.
Read Ars Technica’s Q&A with Elisabeth Braw about Undersea War .
It’s a little-remembered film for most people, but I absolutely love The Burbs . Sure, it’s more Halloween fare than Christmas, but last year I picked The Thing , so clearly “1980s movies for October” is my December viewing MO.
Starring Tom Hanks, Carrie Fisher, and Corey Feldman, this is a dry, hilarious send-up of suburban life with a horror-adjacent mystery that keeps you guessing. (It’s not scary, though.) I hardly ever hear anyone else talk about this movie, but I love it, and it only recently came out in 4K, so I’m taking this opportunity to shout it out.
If you’re a technically minded Ars reader looking for a nice book to snuggle down with over the holidays, David Woods’ How Apollo Flew to the Moon could be just the thing. (There’s also an audiobook version .) Woods has an accessible style that breaks down complex engineering challenges and their solutions into easily digestible chunks that clarify without oversimplifying. He uses that style to take readers on a detailed trip through the machinery of Project Apollo, from the launch facilities and Mission Control all the way to the specific mechanics of how to navigate to and land on the Moon—and, from there, how to return safely to Earth.
Ever wondered about the insane engineering that let the Saturn V’s first stage burn almost 15 tons of fuel every second as it powered the crew into orbit? Or how to pinpoint a spacecraft’s centimeter-precise distance from Earth on its way to the Moon? Or how Apollo crews tracked their own position with stellar navigation, using sextants and star sightings? Or what a REFSMMAT is, or how television transmissions from the Moon worked, or how they got those crazy lunar buggies onto the Moon’s surface? All these questions and more are given beautifully complete and technically satisfying answers, suitable for both the curious layperson and also the interested engineer. Grab this book and stun your family at Christmas with amazing Apollo trivia—as a bonus, you’ll have the knowledge to make your “We never landed on the Moon!” conspiracy theorist uncle so angry that he stops talking and watches football in grumpy silence! Everyone wins!
As someone who grew up in the classic era of 16-bit SNES RPGs, this 40th anniversary tribute to the series’ history is everything I could have ever wanted in a modern entry. I haven’t properly played through a Final Fantasy entry since the days of Final Fantasy X on PlayStation 2, but when friends kept nudging me that this was the perfect “Nick game,” I figured I should probably take a look. There’s a free six-hour demo available on supported platforms if you’re still on the fence about picking this one up, but don’t be surprised if you end up grabbing a copy for yourself.
For the past couple of years, I’ve been transforming my tiny office into a sanctuary in the evenings, since I do most of my writing (and gaming) in here then. Easily my favorite impulse purchase of 2026, the FM-1 is a great gift for curious tinkerers and experienced musicians alike. At around $70 or less, you don’t have to break the bank to get fiddling. A perfectly decent stock synthesizer on its own, the real fun start…

The lead-up to the match at the Stade Vélodrome was marred by confrontations in the stands between the two sets of fans, including the throwing of projectiles and flares.

Magistrates were also looking into allegations of "incitement to hatred after Nazi salutes and provocations from the Bulgarian fans" before the clashes broke out, it told AFP.
French President Emmanuel Macron condemned "in the strongest possible terms ... acts of violence targeting Bulgarian fans", the Élysée Palace said.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova called it "unacceptable" and "shocking".
"The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world," she said in a statement on Facebook.

Macron spoke to his Bulgarian counterpart on the sidelines of a European summit in Brussels , assuring her that "these acts would not go unpunished", the Élysée said.
Several hundred Marseille fans ran from the stand where they were situated about 10 minutes before kick-off, appearing to pursue a group of Levski supporters.

Fighting broke out, with several Marseille fans wearing face coverings, an AFP journalist at the scene said.
"Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder," a source with the Marseille police prefecture told AFP.

She urged European football's governing body UEFA to "check how the safety of the Bulgarian fans at the stadium was ensured".
"We are ready to provide the necessary assistance to our compatriots. This behaviour is unacceptable!" she said.
Security personnel eventually managed to restore calm as the game kicked off on time.
There was another flare-up between opposing fans during half-time, before the match ended 1-0 to the hosts.

"We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable," said Marseille coach Bruno Génésio.

Homes without power, travel disrupted and Macy’s Thanksgiving parade postponed for first time in New York
Storms have flooded communities on the US east coast, knocking out power to nearly a million customers and prompting the first-ever postponement of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City.
High winds and flooding hammered both coasts, disrupting holiday travel. More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday evening, with the majority in east coast states, according to the outage tracking website PowerOutage.us. More than 2,200 flights to or from US destinations were delayed and more than 400 were cancelled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.
Macy’s postponed the annual Thanksgiving parade until Saturday because of concerns about how the parade’s large balloons would fare in the windswept canyons between Manhattan’s skyscrapers.
Torrential rain, high winds and flooding pounded sections of the east coast. New Jersey was under a state of emergency, along with parts of New York. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic and southern New England.
People were rescued from their cars in New York City because of flooding, said the mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities.
Strong winds and flooding disrupted train lines, toppled trees and caused power outages on Thanksgiving night, New York City emergency management officials said. Several scaffolding structures collapsed in the wind, but no injuries were reported.
The storms also flooded areas from North Carolina through to New Jersey as high tide rolled in. Roads were closed, and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water.
Avalon, New Jersey, was seeing some of the worst flooding in its history, said Scott J Wahl, the borough’s business administrator.
“Not quite Hurricane Sandy,” Wahl said, referring to the benchmark storm for his village on the far south end of New Jersey’s Atlantic coast.
Flood waters washed debris over the road, and a few drivers were rescued after driving around barricades into the waters, but no injuries were reported, Wahl said.
Lance Miller, 54, said flood waters in his Ocean City, New Jersey, neighbourhood were about a foot deep and that driving to the nearest supermarket would probably “destroy your car”.
Miller said he would be staying indoors and having Thanksgiving dinner with his wife and daughter. But he said some of his friends were “not so lucky” and had flooding inside their homes.
The Margate City fire department near Atlantic City, New Jersey posted video on Facebook of water pouring through the city’s streets, even before heavy rains started.
A firefighter said the tide was coming in ferociously, even with an hour to go before its peak. Water closed in on houses, and sandbags were piled in front of businesses.
Some highways and bridges were temporarily closed. The nearly 18-mile (29-km) Chesapeake Bay bridge-tunnel in southern Virginia was closed for several hours on Thursday morning because of high winds, while NC 12, the only highway connecting Hatteras Island on the North Carolina Outer Banks to the mainland, was closed after seawater breached the dunes and covered the two-lane highway.
In Maryland, nearly 2 million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were asked to conserve water because of intermittent power disruptions associated with the storm. Baltimore police closed several streets on Thursday night after storm surge caused flooding in waterfront neighborhoods.
The storms also prompted several brief tornado warnings on Thursday, including a rare twister south-east of Seattle, Washington.
The US president, Donald Trump, signed a disaster declaration on Thursday for Florida in response to earlier flooding that damaged hundreds of homes and required water rescues. Trump had approved funding earlier this week, but gathered local officials on Thanksgiving to talk about it in a small signing ceremony at his home in West Palm Beach.
Trump was asked about aid for Thursday’s storms on the east coast. “Well, we’re going to look at that. We have some requests from others,” he said.
Heavy snow fell on parts of Illinois and Missouri with St Louis recording 7.3in (18.5cm) of snowfall. Sainte Genevieve, Missouri, recorded 14in.
The ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, which hosts hockey and other ice skating activities, was empty when the roof caved in at about 3 am, according to the city.
Meanwhile, high-tide driven waves and strong winds caused flooding along the Pacific coast on Thursday. The conditions were expected into Friday, according to the National Weather Service.
Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations in areas from Humboldt county in the far north to Ventura county near Los Angeles.
Video showed a big wave tearing down part of the Pacifica pier in California on Wednesday, sending it into the ocean. Officials had closed the L-shaped pier in the summer after finding cracks.
Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner posted more than a dozen itinerary changes on social media on Thursday morning, starting with one that said trains could not run through San Clemente “due to track damage”. It also suspended service between Irvine and Oceanside because of washouts caused by high tide conditions. Service was further shut down from San Diego north to Oceanside and up to Los Angeles international airport.

Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon loses majority and needs support of Opportunity party to remain in power, or country faces another election
The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.
Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.
On Friday, the electoral commission released the results from nearly 485,000 “special votes” – those cast from overseas or outside a voter’s electorate. National dropped two seats to 40, Labour stayed on 36 seats, the Greens picked up one seat to 17, Act had 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pati Māori five.
The National-led bloc currently has 65 seats. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are needed for a majority.
The revised results mean the National-led coalition has the only realistic path to power – if it can negotiate a deal with Opportunity. If it cannot, New Zealand will probably need to hold another election.
Three electorate seats changed hands after the special votes. Labour won Wairarapa off National with just 81 votes, and took Hamilton East from National with 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour with 1,610 votes.
If National applies for a recount and wins back just one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority and without needing Opportunity. Applications for a recount must be made by 3 December, and results could take another five days.
Special votes in previous elections have favoured the left, and typically have cost the right one or two seats. Until Friday, a question mark hung over whether National would be able to govern comfortably alongside its coalition partners, or whether it would be forced to cut a deal with the Opportunity party – a newcomer centrist party that incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon had previously ruled out working with.
After the election, Luxon softened his stance on his initial rule-out, saying he intended to find common ground with the Opportunity party.
On Friday afternoon, Luxon said National will now begin formal negotiations with New Zealand First, Act and Opportunity, but he cautioned discussions would be “challenging” and could take some time.
“Getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly,” Luxon said. “Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart, or for sending them back to the polls.”
Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, said the prospect of New Zealand heading back to the polls was unprecedented, because negotiations between the four parties will be so complex.
“It’s not a 0% chance, it’s the highest chance we’ve ever had of it being another election,” she said.
Opportunity, led by Auckland businesswoman Qiulae Wong , has long said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats.
After the final results were announced, Wong confirmed she would speak with Luxon and that her party’s bottom-lines – which include climate and environment policies and capping political donations – were non-negotiable.
The party would focus on bringing New Zealanders a stable government, Wong told media, and she did not rule out heading back to the polls.
“Clearly stability is important. But setting that more hopeful and aspirational vision, where we can come together as much as possible as New Zealanders and move forward, I think is the priority,” she said.
Having Opportunity in parliament was a “pivotal moment” for the country, Wong said.
“I have every expectation that we will get in there and we will deliver, regardless of what shape the government takes.”
Previously, Wong has said its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision . Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.
Negotiations with Opportunity could hit a snag with National’s coalition partner New Zealand First. On Friday, Wong confirmed she would not strike a deal if New Zealand First’s leader, the veteran politician Winston Peters, serves as foreign affairs minister – a position he has held on three occasions.
“We think that his behaviour over successive governments is not the kind of behavior that we expect of someone in that position,” she said.
In other points of tension, New Zealand First and Act have diametrically opposed climate policies, and Act are also unlikely to back Opportunity’s drive for political donation reforms.
Greaves said the Opportunity party will have to make difficult decisions over what it is prepared to gain, or lose. “For minor parties, it’s really hard to go into coalition, or be seen as being too close to a major party or propping up a government, and then turn around later and sell their brand ... as separate from that [major] party.”
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said he was proud the party had gained the highest share of the party vote, but was disappointed it could not deliver a change of government.
It is the second election Hipkins has lost, raising questions over his political future. Hipkins said a decision over his leadership would be made after a government had been formed.
New Zealand could be facing weeks of negotiations in what could become its first ever four-party coalition. In 2023, negotiations took five weeks. With Christmas just four weeks away, New Zealand may need to wait until 2027 to know the shape of its next government.

Heavy rain, strong winds and coastal flooding creating hazardous conditions for millions travelling for holiday
King tides and huge waves have been battering both coasts of the US during a turbulent Thanksgiving period, with severe weather threatening millions across the country. Along the California coast, king tides caused considerable damage. In Pacifica, south of San Francisco, large waves battered the coastline on Wednesday, destroying part of a pier and sending debris into the ocean.
The National Weather Service issued coastal flood warnings covering parts of the Pacific coastline and shorelines around San Francisco Bay and San Pablo Bay. Several beachfront properties in Pacifica have already experienced flooding, while authorities in Marin County temporarily issued an evacuation warning for residents of beachfront homes at Stinson Beach.
The high tides also affected southern California. San Diego recorded a tide of 8ft 11in (2.7 metres) on Wednesday morning, while Los Angeles experienced tides reaching approximately 8.19ft, potentially surpassing a record set at the end of October.
King tides are unusually high natural tides that occur when the gravitational forces of the sun and moon combine around their alignment with Earth. Their impact is being heightened by unusually warm Pacific waters associated with the 2026 super El Niño.
A Nor’easter has also been bringing severe weather across the eastern US. The system produced heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding, creating hazardous conditions for millions of Americans travelling to celebrate the holiday.
The severity of the forecast forced an unprecedented decision in New York: Macy’s postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day parade, originally scheduled for Thursday, until Saturday. It was the first time in the event’s history that the parade had been postponed because of weather. The decision was taken to safeguard performers and spectators, particularly given the dangers that powerful gusts pose to the parade’s enormous character balloons.
Meanwhile, significant fresh snowfall during the past week has transformed conditions across several major ski regions in the Alps, providing an excellent early season foundation for the new season. French resorts have been among the biggest beneficiaries. Reported accumulated snow depths on Thursday included approximately 120cm in the Tignes-Val d’Isère area, while substantial snowfall was recorded around Les Deux Alpes, Alpe d’Huez and the Les Trois Vallées. Further snowfall is forecast across parts of France, Switzerland, Italy and Austria, with several resorts expecting additional accumulations over the coming days.

New Zealand's final vote count has left neither bloc with a majority, handing a brand-new centrist party the power to decide who governs.
The Electoral Commission's final tally showed more support for minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. A total of 2.8 million votes were cast.
The tally on Friday, after 400,000 special votes including ballots from New Zealanders abroad, showed Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's National party dropping two seats to finish on 40.
The right-wing bloc now holds 65 seats in the 130-seat parliament, one short of the 66 needed. The left, led by Labour's Chris Hipkins, has 58, with Labour on 36.
That leaves the Opportunity party, an unaligned centrist newcomer with seven seats, as kingmaker. Its support would not be enough to put the left in power, Hipkins conceded on Friday, in an apparent admission of defeat.
Luxon, who ruled out working with Opportunity before the 7 November vote, reversed course saying he was confident of forming a government with Opportunity and his usual partners, the libertarian ACT (13 seats) and the populist NZ First (12).
"These negotiations may be challenging and they could take some time," he said. "But getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly."
Opportunity is led by 38-year-old business consultant Qiulae Wong, who has said she could work with either side. Her party's five "bottom line" policies include tougher climate action and an end to bottom-trawling, both at odds with ACT and NZ First.
Wong also repeated that she will not join a government in which NZ First leader Winston Peters is foreign minister, citing his past remarks in parliament about Asian people. She said she would consider either a full coalition or a "confidence and supply" deal, under which her MPs would back key legislation and decide other bills case by case.
Both major parties took under 30% of the party vote: Labour 29.88% and National 28.35%. Analysts pointed to anger over the cost of living and little enthusiasm for either leader.
PM Luxon survived two confidence votes among his own MPs this year, while Hipkins led Labour to defeat in 2023. Minor parties on both flanks gained ground, with the Greens on 17 seats and Te Pati Māori on five.
Opportunity's rise is striking: it failed three times to enter parliament before Wong took over less than a year ago, and none of its new MPs has served before. If no government can be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh election.

Violent clashes marred a number of European football matches on Thursday night, with French president Emmanuel Macron condemning trouble at Marseille's home game against Levski Sofia.
There were also incidents at games between Turkish side Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Be'er-Sheva in Georgia and Sunderland's 1-1 home draw with Poland's Jagiellonia Bialystok.
In Marseille, the build-up to the Europa League match at the Stade Velodrome was affected by incidents in the stands, including the throwing of projectiles and flares between the two sets of supporters.
With 10 minutes to go until kick-off, several Marseille fans ran from a home stand, appearing to pursue a group of Levski Sofia supporters.
They breached the stand designated for away fans, which housed around 500 supporters of the Bulgarian domestic champions.
"Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder," said the Marseille police prefecture. "Six others were treated on site for various wounds."
Macron spoke to Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev about the incidents, with the French president condemning "with the utmost force these acts of violence, which have no place in sport or in public space", and reassured him that "these acts would not go unpunished".
According to news agency Reuters, Radev thanked Macron for his personal involvement following the "attack on Bulgarian citizens" and for the medical assistance provided to the victims.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova said she found video footage of the incidents "shocking" in a statement posted on social media.
"The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world," she added.
"Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety."
Police response to Besiktas fans' pro-Palestine banner 'unacceptable'
Ligue 1 club Marseille said it was "working to understand the precise circumstances of these incidents".
The police source said all the people injured were Bulgarian and there was "no information at this stage regarding any arrests".
Security personnel managed to restore calm, allowing the game to kick-off on time, although there were a few further flare-ups between the fans, notably during the half-time break in a match Marseille won 1-0.
"It's a very regrettable episode. These are incidents which are unacceptable for football," said Levski Sofia coach Julio Velazquez
Marseille boss Bruno Genesio added: "We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable."
Besiktas fans clash with Georgian police at their game against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er-Sheva
Meanwhile, the Turkish Football Federation has strongly condemned the "unacceptable" actions of Georgian police towards Besiktas fans who unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during their Europa League match against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er-Sheva.
Besiktas say they have lodged a complaint with European football's governing body Uefa over "disproportionate" use of force by Georgian police.
The match had been moved from Istanbul to Batumi, Georgia for safety and security reasons but had to be suspended in the 25th minute after clashes involving Besiktas supporters and local police.
Both the officiating team and the Besiktas players left the field, but play was able to resume 30 minutes later.
"We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, behaviour and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium before and during the Uefa Europa League match," said a statement from the Turkish federation.
Turkish outlet NTV reported that Georgian police had gone into the stands and used pepper spray on the Besiktas fans.
The report added that there were anti-Israeli chants from the Turkish fans and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters to try to calm matters before play restarted.
Hakan Fidan, Turkey's minister of foreign affairs, spoke to his Georgian counterpart Maka Botchorishvili following the incident.
"All necessary steps are being taken to ensure the safety of our citizens and protect their rights," a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
At Sunderland, there were crowd disturbances after Jagiellonia Bialystok fans were found in areas of the Stadium of Light with home fans, despite Uefa having imposed an away supporter ban for the Europa League game.
Police and stewards attended some disruption early on during the match.
"In the build-up to the match, the club had put measures in place in line with this sanction and maintained regular communication with our supporters, Jagiellonia Bialystok and Uefa," said a Sunderland statement.
"Unfortunately, Jagiellonia Bialystok failed to engage and cooperate on this matter.
"We are disappointed that these measures and communications were disregarded by some visiting supporters and we will review the circumstances surrounding their entry into the stadium."

Watch: Roofs torn off and streets under water as severe weather hits the US
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.
Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.
Conditions are forecast now to improve, though the National Weather Service (NWS) cautions that it will take some time. The West Coast has also been affected by its own storms.
Flight disruption also persists, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - which is expected to be another busy travel day.
More than 2,500 flights within, into or out of the US were delayed on Thursday, and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com.
One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.
Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport.
The number of homes reporting power cuts peaked at close to a million on Thursday evening - with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey badly affected.
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. In Maryland, almost two million customers were asked by authorities to limit their water consumption to essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".
Parts of eastern states are under states of emergency, including New York. Organisers of New York City's annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have also postponed the iconic event to Saturday.
On the West Coast, the concern was for exceptionally high tides and the associated risk of flooding.
Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft (2.4m) earlier this week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas.
Watch: Man and dog narrowly escape powerful king tide in Oregon
Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media.
Dramatic footage from Oregon showed a man and a dog being swept into the sea by a fierce, so-called king tide - but both escaped unharmed, police said.
FedEx plane sends dirt flying while overshooting Miami runway
In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.
A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing". No injuries were reported, and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is investigating what happened.
An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.

If the ruling bloc cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.
It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.
The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.
A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.
Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.
"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More New Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes – one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative.
Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.
Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.
"There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.
Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.
But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.
Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.
Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.

Iran denied responsibility on Thursday for drone strikes on Kuwait that killed two Italian nationals, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calling the accusations baseless and proposing a joint investigation with Rome and Kuwait City.
Araghchi spoke by telephone with his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts, Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah and Antonio Tajani, and later wrote on X that the incident was "suspicious and looks like a preecooked recipe for war."
"We stand ready to cooperate with Kuwait and Italy to determine the cause of the incident," he added.
Tajani had earlier told the Italian Senate that several Iranian drones struck Kuwaiti military facilities at around 2 pm local time (12 pm CET), including an air defence radar centre where two Italian specialists employed by arms company Rheinmetall were working.
Kuwait's Al-Sabah condemned the attack as "a heinous Iranian aggression" and offered condolences to Italy.
Senior spokesperson for Iran's armed forces Abolfazl Shekarchi flatly denied any Iranian military operation in the region and accused the US and Israel of staging a false flag attack to destabilise the area.
IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency went further, citing an unnamed security source who alleged that Ukraine had deployed a network of thousands of drones across the region, including in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. It provided no evidence.
The Iran embassy in Rome separately issued a statement categorically rejecting any Iranian role and warning against attempts to widen the war.
Saudi Arabia called for an immediate halt to Iranian attacks and said it held Tehran responsible for the consequences of its actions. Bahrain asked the UN Security Council to hold Iran accountable and demanded compensation for the damage.
Qatar warned that repeated strikes on Kuwait risked undermining diplomatic efforts to reduce regional tensions. The UAE, Syria and Jordan also condemned the attack.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for increased pressure on Tehran and said Gulf security was directly linked to Europe's security.
Iran has repeatedly struck Arab Gulf states with drones and missiles since the start of the war, saying it has targeted military bases and US-linked facilities, with Kuwait and Bahrain among the most frequently targeted countries.
Tehran has urged its neighbours not to allow their territory to be used for attacks against Iran.
Iran's army confirmed a separate drone attack on Kuwait's Ali Al Salem base earlier in November.
Tajani had informed the Italian parliament on 8 October of a decision to relocate most of its troops from Kuwait, with only around 10 military personnel remaining in the country at the time of the attack.

Jangling keys has turned into a symbol of protest against Spain's housing struggles
Spain's main party leaders have made their last pitch to voters in a fractious final TV debate that focused heavily on the country's housing crisis.
Spaniards go to the ballot box on Sunday, with opinion polls suggesting Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will fail to extend his eight years in office.
The debate on Thursday night marked the culmination of a campaign, which has been defined by the din of house keys being jangled in symbolic protest, rather than any carefully crafted words of politicians.
The struggle many face in opening the door to an affordable home has led to demonstrations filling plazas across the country.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the conservative People's Party (PP), who is poised to replace Sánchez, told viewers he would build a million new homes.
The PP, which is narrowly projected to be the largest party, is poised to form a government with the Vox party which is polling in third place.
If Vox do win a share of power at a national level, it would be the first time for the far right in Spain's 50 years of democracy since Francisco Franco's dictatorship.
Vox's leader Santiago Abascal told the debate only he cared about those who had the greatest housing need.
Ada Colau, who heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Broad Front, said taxing rich and exploitative landlords was urgently required.
Rejecting criticism that he had failed to tackle the country's housing problem, Sanchez talked up his recent emergency measures designed to protect tenants and cap rents.
Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake
Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
Sparking the protests in September was the eviction – and subsequent death in hospital – of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal (no relation to Santiago). She could not afford a tripling of her rent in Madrid.
But it is Spain's third city, Valencia, that is at the heart of what many call a full-blown housing crisis.
"We want to live together but we look at the prices of property and it's impossible," says 25-year-old Nuria Cifuentes from the city.
She and her boyfriend Miguel Martínez work as sports journalists but are still living with their respective families because of the high cost of renting a flat, even with their combined salaries.
Nuria and Miguel want to live together but feel they are priced out
"Half of what we earn would go on rent of more than €1,000 a month," Miguel, 26, says.
We meet the couple outside Valencia's futuristic science museum, whose distinctive design is often compared to the skeleton of a whale.
This coastal location has witnessed the biggest rise in rent prices of any major Spanish city over the past half a decade, according to official data from the INE, the national statistics office.
One study from the city's Polytechnic University put the increase at 78% between 2020 and 2025.
Sánchez called a snap election after Congress rejected his emergency housing reforms.
A revised version was later pushed through a parliamentary standing committee – restricting evictions and capping rent rises – but opponents say he has had eight years to sort the problem and has resolutely failed.
Nuria and Miguel say the soaring cost of housing means that life is on pause for them, as they're unable to make concrete plans for the future.
"Maybe we want to have kids, maybe we want to actually buy somewhere, but there are so many unknowns that all I see is a black expanse," Nuria says.
"The problem here is that our salaries are very low and life is very expensive."
The wider cost of living is the second most important issue for Spaniards, according to numerous surveys carried out during this election period.
Wages failing to catch up with rising prices – despite Spain's GDP growing faster than the three bigger EU countries, Germany, France and Italy – is another reason why Sánchez's PSOE party is only sitting in second place, according to final opinion polls.
Feijóo is said to be most likely to form the next government with the support of Vox under its leader Santiago Abascal.
Having called access to housing a "vital emergency", Feijóo wants to cut taxes for under-40s buying their first home and scrap the Socialists' housing law.
Pedro Sánchez (left) and Núñez Feijóo on screen during the leaders' debate
On housing, Vox has gone further than PSOE and PP, promising to prioritise Spaniards over foreigners for social housing and housing aid, as well as other welfare benefits.
On immigration, identified as the third most important issue, Vox advocates deportations for criminals from abroad and, most controversially, a policy of remigration for foreign nationals who "do not contribute to Spain".
Daniel, 30, is unemployed and says he is ready to vote for Vox for the first time
Opponents of Vox say those who have arrived legally and live and work peacefully risk being forced out.
But 30-year-old Daniel, who is currently unemployed, says he is ready to give his vote to Vox for the first time.
"First of all, it's immigration. It's bad in Spain today – that's why I'm going further to the right," he says.
"The left helps those who don't work, but we need people who work and contribute. We need to give less aid to people who come from abroad and don't contribute."
"We are almost being charged to just breathe at the moment," he says.
We meet Daniel coming out of a shopping centre. We explain that other people we met in the previous hour who told us they support Vox did not want to give their name or be photographed.
Is he proud to be voting far right, or does he have concerns about his choice?
"I'll say it like it is… I've always been centre right but have gone to the extreme right… I've decided to choose nationalism."
Spain's control of its borders was criticised by 22 of its 26 EU partners in the summer, in a rebuke to Sánchez.
In July more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta in just two days.
Sánchez has argued the foreign workforce is essential to Spain's economic growth, and in April announced plans to give half a million undocumented migrants legal status.
Maria and German feel they have little choice but to back the Socialist party
In the final days of the campaign, Sánchez has made a flurry of new spending announcements amounting to billions of euros, promising wage rises in the public sector, higher pensions and discounted transport.
Twenty-year-old student María García says she welcomes the promises but asks why they have come so late in the day.
"The Socialist party have been in power for eight years and now suddenly, during the election campaign, they are passing a lot of progressive laws – which I agree with – but isn't that hypocritical?" she says.
"I don't really have a choice but to vote for them, but come on – you had eight years to do all this!"
Maria's sentiments chime with those of her boyfriend German Martinez, 18.
I put it to them that nearly a fifth of Spaniards are said to be choosing Vox and a number of studies say it's set to be the top choice of first-time voters.
"I believe Spain is stepping into the lion's den because we are scared of the dogs outside. We need to be careful," she says.
"People need to inform themselves – just listen to what these guys say. That 20% of Spanish people agree with them really scares me."
Sánchez will be hoping that fear among the undecided of a national government that includes Vox will save him.
He is a great political survivor, but even if his party wins the most votes he has no obvious path to build a majority.
The man who called a snap election over housing now faces his own eviction - from office.

Matt Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch, admits making offensive remark and says he was referencing assault survivor’s ‘strikingly attractive get-up’
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
A former Murdoch media executive has admitted he said Grace Tame “must be looking to be raped again” at an event, after the former Australian of the year overheard the comment and confronted him.
Tame, a child sexual assault victim survivor who was Australian of the year in 2021 for her advocacy work, revealed in an opinion piece for Crikey that she heard Matt Handbury make the comment to another man at a function last week.
“That’s Grace Tame. Look at her with her tits hanging out. She must be looking to be raped again,” Handbury said, according to Tame’s piece published on Friday.
Tame wrote that she didn’t realise that the man was Handbury until a bystander told her. He introduced himself as “Matt” after she confronted him.
The 77-year-old is Rupert Murdoch’s nephew and the former owner of Murdoch Magazines and Murdoch Books. He is now on the board of The Sydney Retreat, a rehab centre.
Tame said Handbury conceded at the UNSW event – where former military lawyer David McBride was presented with an award – that he had made the comment.
The following day, Handbury sent an email to Tame, seen by Guardian Australia, in which he also admitted he said “she must be looking to be raped again”. Tame was 15 when repeatedly sexually abused by her 58-year-old maths teacher, Nicolaas Bester, who was later convicted and jailed. In 2019, Tame won a supreme court exemption which overturned a Tasmanian law that had until then gagged her from speaking about her experiences of assault.
“He [Handbury] didn’t say she must be looking to get raped,” Tame told Guardian Australia. “He said she must be looking to get raped again . Therefore evidencing his prior knowledge of what I have been through.”
Tame said that the comment “activated really deep seated trauma and there are consequences to that”.
“It’s really destabilising and disorienting because your body is essentially your abused self and it is in total survival mode,” she said.
Handbury said in the email to Tame: “I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up. It was meant to be in appreciation in a male-to-male exchange. I can see that might be offensive in the context of suggesting a woman is making herself attractive to men in some titillating fashion.”
“I also said: ‘She must be looking to be raped again.’ This was certainly meant for no one’s ears but my friend. However it was in poor taste. In fact in highly objectionable taste and I regretted it as soon as I got out into the fresh air. Thank you for calling me out.
“Some men, obviously including myself, are prone to finding suggestive humour in the wrong places. I deeply regret my letting such bad habits get in the way of common courtesy, respect and decency. Please accept my humblest apologies.
“Thank you for opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink on Friday. But no one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous that night.”
Tame wrote in her Crikey piece that “what makes this provocation especially egregious is that Matt didn’t reference an imagined harm, but a very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about”.
“It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?” she wrote.
“This isn’t about Matt personally; it’s about a broader culture of normalised violence. However, part of that culture is the self-censorship that protects people like him.”
Tame referred to research that suggested 35% of Australian men believe women’s rights have come too far, adding that “research has repeatedly shown that misogynistic attitudes are a broad predictor of violent extremism and prevalent among men of all ages.”
Tame told Guardian Australia she often faced re-traumatising behaviour from men.
“I’m tired. I’m tired of the maltreatment. I’m tired of the gaslighting. I’m tired of being baited and then have people be shocked why I would be angry or re-traumatised,” she said on Friday.
Tame thanked bystanders at the event who supported her following Handbury’s comment.
The chief executive of Full Stop Australia, Karen Bevan, called on people to speak up if they heard similar comments because “we all have the power to shift this”.
“If one of the most recognised survivor advocates in the country can be spoken about like this at an event honouring a whistleblower in a room full of people, you can be assured this behaviour is normalised,” Bevan said.
“Things like this do get said in workplaces, pubs, group chats and boardrooms across the country, where no one is recording, and no one writes about it afterwards.”
Crikey reported Handbury told the outlet in further correspondence that he didn’t recall using the phrase “tits hanging out”.
“It doesn’t sound like me. I think I said something along the lines of ‘Did you see Grace Tame? What a hot outfit’ followed by the terrible reference to rape.”
Handbury was contacted for comment as was The Sydney Retreat.

Tame says her "whole body was prickling with distress" over what Handbury said.
An Australian former media executive has admitted he said a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.
Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.
In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame said she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.
Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.
Matt Handbury is the nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms
Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.
She said the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.
"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.
"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."
The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".
"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'
He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".
"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.
Handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.
Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".
"It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"
From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.
"They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.
"I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.
"I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line .

Emmanuel Macron said it would be a "strategic mistake" to reduce EU spending
European Union (EU) leaders have deferred negotiations on its long-term budget after tensions surfaced over the bloc's spending priorities and aid for Ukraine.
Tense talks on the 2028-34 budget ended after 12 hours on Thursday at a summit in Brussels, with some members walking out of negotiations that will resume in December.
Divisions were largely split along the lines of countries, including France and Italy, wanting to approve a higher-spending proposal against those advocating for financial restraint, with Germany chief among them.
Many members want the budget locked in ahead of several high-stakes elections held across Europe in 2027, including in France.
Countries remain divided over a proposal to provide Ukraine with an additional loan of €45bn (£37.6bn), split between non-military and military funding.
Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary have objected to the loan, but German Chancellor Frederich Merz said uniform EU agreement was a condition for approving the broader budget.
"I stand by my view that aid for Ukraine must be supported by the European Union as a whole," Merz told reporters.
"The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."
Bulgaria, which previously opposed the plan, said it would agree to fund part of the loan that commits non-military financial support to Kyiv, marking a small sign of progress emerging from the special summit of the European Council.
EU members have been wrangling over the long-term budget after the European Commission submitted a €2tn proposal earlier this year, with some countries objecting to high levels of spending.
Those advocating higher spending want the funds to future-proof industries such as farming and invest in regional development. Fiscally cautious countries want to avoid amassing ballooning debt.
Thursday's talks were set up by the European Council to unblock the impasse, with a proposal to reduce spending by approximately €220bn to €230bn.
Under the current proposal, the budget totals €1.582tn, which includes €140bn to repay pandemic-era borrowing.
Four countries wanting to rein in the budget, including Denmark and Austria, walked out of negotiations after several hours of meetings.
Merz said there was "new movement" towards reducing the size of the EU budget, though he added "we are not there yet" when he confirmed that a new round of negotiations would not take place in Brussels on Friday.
European budgets requires approval from all 27 countries, with each country effectively holding veto power.
French President Emmanuel Macron said it would be a "strategic mistake" to lower long-term spending.
France's forthcoming presidential election came into focus during the EU budget talks, with frontrunner Marine Le Pen calling the talks an "underhanded political manoeuvring to thwart the democratic will of the French people".
Last month, Le Pen announced she would significantly reduce French aid to Ukraine and EU contributions if she were to win the presidency.
Macron addressed Le Pen's remarks on the sidelines of the Brussels summit, saying: "It is an odd kind of arrogance to behave as if she is already in charge of France's destiny because, as things stand, she has not been elected."
Once the talks concluded, the European Council announced a two-day summit on 17 and 18 December would revive budget negotiations.
Spanish economist Pablo Hernández de Cos was also named as the next President of the European Central Bank, replacing Christine Lagarde from February 2027.

Violent clashes at two European football matches have stoked concerns about fan violence and prompted the leaders of France and Bulgaria to condemn behaviour that had “no place in civilized Europe”.
Images showed masked ⁠and bloodied fans wielding improvised weapons and metal pipes during a brawl at a UEFA Europa League match on Wednesday evening between Marseille and Levski Sofia, which the Bulgarian club said began when their fans were attacked by supporters of the French side.
A photographer working for the Reuters news agency ⁠said the clashes at the Stade Velodrome in Marseille had started after a supporter from the visitors’ stand made a Nazi salute.
Clashes also broke out at a Europa League match in the Georgian city of Batumi between Turkiye’s Besiktas and Israel’s Hapoel Be’er Sheva, forcing the referee to suspend the match for 30 minutes.
European football’s governing body UEFA told Reuters its disciplinary body “would assess the match reports before considering any potential ‌next steps”.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he and French President Emmanuel Macron spoke by phone and condemned the violence at the Marseille-Levski Sofia match, in which Marseille police said 11 Bulgarian fans were hurt, five of whom were taken to hospital.
“We share the position that aggression and violence have no place in civilized Europe,” Radev said on Facebook.
“I thank President Macron for his personal commitment to this case, for the medical care provided to the injured by the French authorities, for the measures taken to ensure the safety of Bulgarian citizens, and for the perpetrators to be held accountable.”
Macron said he had condemned “with the utmost ⁠force” acts of violence targeting Bulgarian fans, which he said had “no place in sport or in ⁠public space”, and told Radev they would not go unpunished.
A protest was planned in front of the French embassy in Sofia ⁠later on Friday.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said: “Violence, racial hatred and provocation have no place in our stadiums.”
Manuel Bompard, a French lawmaker for the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party in the Marseille department, commented on a video on social media appearing to show a Levski fan performing a Nazi salute.
“Congrats to the Marseille fans who responded with an antifascist chant,” Bompard wrote on X. “The far-right has no place in our stadiums!”
Levski Sofia, which lost the match 1-0, said masked fans had attacked its supporters with batons and flares. Some had let off flares and tried to get through ⁠the barrier as security staff tried to hold them back.
Images showed fans attacking each other through a netted fence separating sections of the stadium.
Before Thursday’s match, French authorities had introduced a sevenfold reduction of ticket sales to Levski supporters and imposed additional restrictions on their movement to and ⁠around the stadium, aiming to curb risks of violence.
The Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it would request a ⁠thorough investigation. Marseille said it would conduct its own analysis and was working closely ⁠with law enforcement.
The match between Besiktas and Hapoel Be’er Sheva had been moved from Istanbul for what UEFA said were safety and security reasons.
Clashes in the stands led referee Morten Krogh to suspend the match in the 26th minute, and it resumed after a 30-minute delay. Georgian police entered the stands, and television footage showed one ‌fan being carried out on a stretcher.
Turkish outlet NTV reported that police used pepper spray. Besiktas condemned what it called “disproportionate force” by security staff and said a number of fans had been denied entry. Besiktas went on to win 2-1.
Turkish Football Federation chair Ibrahim Haciosmanoglu defended the ‌decision ‌to keep Israeli clubs out of Turkiye following Israel’s invasion of Gaza in 2023 after the deadly Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.

Le Pen has vowed to end financial aid to Ukraine, which is still fighting to hold back the Russian advance, and slash French contributions to ⁠the EU budget.
French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters that he had until the end of the year to strike a deal.
"After 31 December, I will no longer be in a position, politically or democratically, to reopen discussions on the budget and bring them to a conclusion, as we will be ​entering a period far too close to the presidential election in France," Macron said.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also mentioned the end of the 2026 as the deadline that leaders were ‌working towards.
The talks on Thursday, while inconclusive, are to help the chair of EU summits, Antonio Costa , present a budget proposal in the coming weeks on which EU governments might agree at a meeting on December 17 and 18.
"Even negotiations that do not lead to the desired outcome or the most positive result possible are necessary to make progress," Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker told reporters. "Even though we were apparently ‌unable to bridge our differences today, we may know what is necessary to ensure success next time."
Under the current proposal, the seven-year budget totals €1.582 trillion, which includes €140 billion to repay pandemic-era borrowing. The biggest line item is around €740 billion to support European farmers and help ​the poorest regions of the EU catch up with the richer ones.
Leaders must also sort out how to continue financing Ukraine as Kyiv defends itself against a Russian invasion that started in 2022.
The 2028-2034 budget draft includes up to €100 billion for Ukraine, which diplomats say falls well short of the country's needs.
The talks also cover aid to Kyiv in ​2027 because a proposed loan intended to raise funds for Ukraine would be borrowed against the EU's current budget, which expires at the end of next year. The EU wants to borrow €45 ​billion and lend it to Ukraine , to be repaid only when Russia pays war reparations.
In 2027, non-EU countries such as Britain, ​Norway, Japan , Switzerland and Canada are expected to provide another €25 billion for Ukraine. The combined €70 billion would cover the funding gap that Ukraine faces next year.
One of the fights is over whether all EU countries should contribute to the €45 billion ​loan to Ukraine.
Slovakia, the Czech Republic , Hungary and Bulgaria object, but Germany and several other countries have made participation a condition of a broader budget deal.
"For me, there is a link between our support for Ukraine and the European budget," Merz said. "The European Union comprises of 27 member states, not 23 or 24."
The four objecting countries are major net beneficiaries of EU spending. The debate is a microcosm of ongoing divisions between countries that contribute more to the EU budget than they get from it, such as Germany, Sweden , the Netherlands and Finland , and those that on balance receive more ⁠than they pay.
The net contributors want EU budget reductions, which would lower their contributions, and urge that spending prioritise making the EU more competitive against rivals like the US and China rather than subsidising European agriculture and poor regions.
The net ⁠beneficiaries say that the budget should ​have money for both aims, and believe doing that would sustain public support for the EU in the face of far-right political parties' rising popularity throughout Europe.

Conservative PM Luxon and populist coalition partners face negotiations with centrist kingmaker.
The final results of New Zealand’s November 7 election offer no clear path to forming a government, suggesting tricky political wrangling is likely in the weeks ahead.
The results, released on Friday, showed that the ruling centre-right coalition led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s conservative National Party has fallen one seat short of a parliamentary majority.
Luxon has led New Zealand since 2023, but National and its junior partners – the populist New Zealand First and libertarian ACT – won just 65 seats between them. National secured 40 seats while ACT and New Zealand First won 13 seats and 12 seats, respectively.
The result reflects a loss of support for Luxon driven by a stagnant economy, and leaves the former businessman and his coalition partners to seek additional help to secure a majority.
“New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together and will last for the full term,” Luxon told a news conference on Friday.
Labour, the largest opposition party, won 36 seats, leaving it far below the 66-seat threshold in the 130-member parliament.
The results appear to position Qiulae Wong’s centrist Opportunity Party, which clinched 7 seats, as kingmaker. However, talks with the conservative and populist incumbents are likely to prove tricky.
The former consultant has promised a universal basic income of up to NZ$370 (US$208) a week, greater action on climate change, a ban on bottom-trawling fishing, and healthcare reforms.
She has also campaigned for a kinder approach to politics. Wong has pledged to do “everything we can” to ensure a stable government.
Her style contrasts with that of potential suitors such as Winston Peters of New Zealand First. The controversial foreign minister has called opponents “morons” and drew shock earlier this year when he told a Chinese-born lawmaker to “go back to your country”. His party promises to tighten immigration flows and withdraw from the Paris Climate Accord.
Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour of ACT campaigned against a greater governance role for the Indigenous Maori minority and has promised massive cuts to state spending.
Failure to meet an agreement could see Kiwis return to the polls next year.
Luke Oldfield, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, told Reuters news agency a deal was likely, although it could be challenging.
“I don’t know exactly what kind of shape that will be yet, but it’ll be highly likely that there will be a right bloc formed and not a second election,” he said.
